posts.title: Props removed without coordination and ad-hoc masonry bracing: two recurring temporary works failures
posts.excerpt: CROSS continues to receive reports of temporary works being altered or improvised on site without design, without Temporary Works Coordinator involvement, and without formal change control. A raking strut removed because it obstructed a pour, and timber bracing fixed to masonry walls without calculation, both illustrate the same gap: temporary stability treated as informal site kit rather than a managed system under BS 5975-1:2024.
posts.linkedinReady:
A temporary works scheme is not complete until the last prop is struck under controlled conditions. Removing one element because it is in the way, or improvising timber bracing on a partially built masonry wall, is still a design change — and design changes need coordination.

Two recent CROSS reports make the point clearly for contractors and Temporary Works Coordinators.

In CROSS Report 1388 a retaining wall of 600 mm pipe piles with raking props was holding a slope until a transfer slab could be built. One strut obstructed the contractor’s work on the slab, so it was removed. The result was an unsafe section of temporary works. The resident engineer had to instruct remedial works and insist that the slab be completed and the wall stabilised before any further controlled removal. The Expert Panel’s message was unambiguous: any proposed change to the design — authorised or otherwise — must be agreed with the principal designer and principal contractor; the Temporary Works Coordinator should be consulted; and on complex sites daily coordination meetings exist precisely to surface these sequencing conflicts before operatives take matters into their own hands.

In CROSS Report 1525 a reporter raised continuing concern about ad-hoc timber bracing systems used to support masonry walls during construction. These arrangements often lack design, calculations or competent oversight. The reporter had personal experience of a life-changing injury from a masonry wall collapse. The Expert Panel noted that partially completed masonry walls remain vulnerable to overturning from modest wind, impact or construction loads, and that improvised bracing can give a false sense of security while introducing unassessed failure modes. Temporary stability of masonry must be identified as temporary works, managed under BS 5975 procedures, and supported by proven or designed systems rather than site improvisation.

Both cases sit inside the same control framework that contractors already operate under CDM 2015 and BS 5975-1:2024:

• Treat every temporary support — prop, strut, bracing, crash deck or working platform — as an item on the Temporary Works Register.
• Do not remove, modify or load any temporary works element without the Temporary Works Coordinator’s knowledge and a documented change or permit process.
• Require design (or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity) before installation of temporary restraint to masonry or other free-standing elements.
• Use daily coordination and task planning to surface spatial conflicts early so that alternative sequences or temporary works redesigns can be agreed before work is forced into an unsafe condition.
• Competence matters: the person authorising a change or completing an inspection must be competent for that class of temporary works.

Educational only — not for construction; subject to the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: CROSS 1388 — temporary works strut removed prematurely
body.p: A resident engineer reported a substantial building project where a retaining wall of 600 mm pipe piles with raking props was containing a slope until a transfer slab could be constructed. One of the raking struts was obstructing the contractor’s work on the slab and was removed, leaving an unsafe section of temporary works. The reporter instructed remedial works and required the transfer slab to be completed and the pipe-pile wall stabilised before any further controlled removal of props. CROSS published the report (ID 1388) on 26 August 2025.

body.h: Expert Panel comments on change control
body.p: The Expert Panel observed that numerous failures have resulted from changes — authorised or otherwise — to both temporary and permanent works, often with unforeseen consequences. Any proposed change should be agreed with the principal designer and principal contractor. Where a Temporary Works Coordinator is appointed, they should be consulted so that an alternative solution can be coordinated. The contractor remains responsible for the temporary works; if progress is obstructed, the reason should be understood and the deviation communicated through the temporary works procedure rather than resolved by unilateral removal. Daily coordination meetings and detailed spatial task planning are practical tools for identifying such conflicts before operatives act.

body.h: CROSS 1525 — ad-hoc temporary bracing of masonry walls
body.p: A reporter raised concern about the continued use of ad-hoc timber bracing systems supporting masonry walls during construction. These systems frequently lack proper temporary works design, calculations or oversight, leaving structures unstable and workers exposed to serious risk. The reporter had suffered a life-changing injury from a preventable masonry wall collapse. CROSS published the report (ID 1525) on 13 May 2026. The Expert Panel confirmed that partially completed masonry walls are vulnerable to overturning from relatively modest loads (wind, impact or construction activity) and that improvised bracing can provide a false sense of security while remaining unassessed.

body.h: Control expectations under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM
body.p: Temporary stability of masonry and the controlled removal or modification of props and struts are temporary works. They belong on the Temporary Works Register, require competent Temporary Works Coordinator oversight, and must not be altered by informal site decision. BS 5975-1:2024 sets out the management procedures; CDM 2015 requires the principal contractor to plan, manage and monitor the construction phase so that it is carried out without risks to health or safety so far as is reasonably practicable, and to ensure that the stability of any structure is not compromised. Design (or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity), formal change control, and competent inspection close the hold points that prevent these recurring failures.

CROSS Safety Report 1388, “Temporary works strut removed prematurely”, published 26 August 2025 (cross-safety.org). CROSS Safety Report 1525, “Concerns with temporary bracing of masonry walls during construction”, published 13 May 2026 (cross-safety.org). BS 5975-1:2024 Temporary works — Management procedures for the control of temporary works. Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015. HSE temporary works guidance (hse.gov.uk/construction/safetytopics/temporary-works.htm).

posts.title: No design, no calculated load, incompetent inspection: the Paxton House platform collapse
posts.excerpt: HSE’s June 2026 prosecution of the Paxton House temporary platform collapse underlines a recurring control failure: temporary structures used without design, without a calculated safe load, and inspected by someone who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM require the opposite — a live register, competent oversight and verified capacity before use.
posts.linkedinReady:
A temporary platform is still a structure. If it carries load, it needs design, a calculated capacity, and a competent person to inspect it before use.

HSE’s June 2026 prosecution of the Paxton House case makes the point plainly. During refurbishment in the City of London, temporary wooden platforms were built under openings being cut through concrete floors. Debris and 16 kg cores accumulated. On 23 February 2024 a platform gave way, collapsing onto a drilling operative who was working directly beneath it. He sustained fractures to his neck and back and a bleed on the brain; he has not returned to construction work.

HSE found:
• no design for the platforms
• no calculation of a safe loading level
• an inspection form completed by someone who was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator
• verbal instructions to “clear the platforms and not overload them” with no known safe load and no monitoring that the instruction was followed

Roots Contractors Ltd (principal contractor) was fined £19,333 plus costs for breaching CDM 2015 Regulation 16(2). Diacutt Ltd was fined £13,000 plus costs for breaching Regulation 15(2). The hearing was at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 11 June 2026; HSE published the outcome on 15 June 2026.

The same control gaps appear across recent CROSS reports and other HSE cases: temporary works treated as informal site kit rather than structures subject to BS 5975-1:2024 management procedures. Proprietary props, timber platforms, crash decks and debris boards are only as safe as the full load path and the process that puts them into service.

For contractors, site managers and Temporary Works Coordinators:

• Put every temporary platform, crash deck or load-bearing board on the Temporary Works Register. “Simple” does not mean exempt.
• Require a design (or a standard solution with documented capacity) and a calculated safe load before the item is used.
• Ensure the person completing inspections is competent for that class of temporary works — availability is not competence.
• Close the permit-to-load / hold point before operatives work under or on the structure.
• Monitor that debris is cleared to the design load; a verbal instruction without a number and without checking is not control.

Educational only — not for construction; subject to the project temporary works procedure.

https://www.temporaryworksconsulting.com/news.html

#TemporaryWorks #BS5975 #HSE #CROSS #WorkingPlatforms #TWC #CDM #ConstructionSafety #StructuralStability #Competence

body.p: On 23 February 2024, during a refurbishment project at Paxton House in the City of London, openings were being cut through five concrete floors to form a service riser. Principal contractor Roots Contractors Ltd instructed carpenters to build temporary wooden platforms under the openings to collect 16 kg concrete cores and debris. A drilling operative working for Diacutt Ltd was cutting an opening on the third floor, directly beneath one of the platforms, when it collapsed. Debris and the platform fell onto him. He described being “folded up like a concertina.” Injuries included fractures to the neck and back and a bleed on the brain. He has not returned to work in construction.

There was no design for the temporary platforms and no calculation of a safe loading level. An inspection form was completed but did not identify the design gap; the person completing it was not a competent Temporary Works Coordinator. Although there had been a verbal instruction to clear the platforms regularly and not overload them, no safe load was known and there was no monitoring that the platforms were cleared. Risk assessments and method statements were inconsistent, supervision of the drilling team was lacking in the week before and on the day of the incident, and coordination of who should be working where was unclear.

At Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 11 June 2026, Roots Contractors Ltd of Ewell, Surrey pleaded guilty to breaching Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 Regulation 16(2) and was fined £19,333 plus £5,548 costs. Diacutt Ltd of Croydon pleaded guilty to Regulation 15(2) and was fined £13,000 plus £5,548 costs. HSE published the prosecution on 15 June 2026. HSE inspector Lucy Ellison-Dunn stated that temporary structures must be properly designed and constructed to withstand any foreseeable load, and that contractors must have arrangements to plan, manage and monitor the work so that workers can carry it out safely.

body.h: Control lessons under BS 5975-1:2024 and CDM
body.p: The case sits alongside recent CROSS reports that show temporary works still being treated as informal site kit rather than structures subject to formal management procedures. A platform that carries debris is a temporary structure. It belongs on the Temporary Works Register. It needs a design or an accepted standard solution with documented capacity, a calculated safe load, installation verification, and inspection by a person competent for that class of work. Verbal instructions without numbers and without monitoring do not satisfy the duty to plan, manage and monitor under CDM or the management procedures in BS 5975-1:2024. The Temporary Works Coordinator must close the relevant hold points before the structure is loaded or worked under.

HSE Media Centre, “Two firms fined after worker fractures neck during platform collapse”, 15 June 2026 (press.hse.gov.uk). Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015. BS 5975-1:2024 Temporary works — Management procedures for the control of temporary works. HSE guidance on temporary works (hse.gov.uk/construction/safetytopics/temporary-works.htm).
